### VS Codium, a local model, and then the straight line

## 1 · This one is longer than the others

This is the only pre-session that installs anything. Sessions 2 to 6 assume
everything below is working, and none of them will ask you to install again.

**The work, and roughly how long each part takes:**

| | | |
|---|---|---|
| **1** | Install VS Codium | 10 min |
| **2** | Install Python and make a virtual environment | 30 min |
| **3** | Clone the course and run the verification suite | 10 min |
| **4** | Install Ollama, pull Qwen 2.5 Coder, configure Continue | 30 min |
| **5** | Read the assigned chapters | 60 min |
| **6** | Work through the pandas section, at the keyboard | 30 min |
| **7** | Read the inference section, and attempt the self-check | 30 min |

::: {.warn}
Budget three hours, once. Doing it in the ten minutes before class does not
work, and every subsequent session depends on it. Steps 1 to 4 never have to be
repeated.
:::

## 2 · The toolchain, and why these four

::: {.tight}
| | | |
|---|---|---|
| **1** | **VS Codium** | the editor — VS Code with the telemetry removed |
| **2** | **Python 3.12+** | in a virtual environment, one per project |
| **3** | **Ollama + Qwen 2.5 Coder** | a language model running **on your machine** |
| **4** | **Continue** | that model, inside the editor, beside the file |
:::

::: {.step}
All four are open source, none requires an account or a subscription, and after
setup **none of them needs a network connection**. That is not frugality — each
choice teaches something the alternative would hide.
:::

## Why VS Codium rather than VS Code

Visual Studio Code is developed in the open under a permissive licence. The
binary Microsoft distributes is not the same artefact: it adds telemetry and
ships under a proprietary licence, and its extension marketplace is a Microsoft
service with its own terms. **VS Codium is the identical source, compiled
without the telemetry and the branding.**

::: {.step}
The practical reason is the habit rather than this course's data. The teaching
data here is generated on your laptop and could not matter less. The habit is
for the working file you will one day open under a non-disclosure agreement or a
research ethics protocol. An editor that reports usage to a third party should
be a decision you make once, deliberately — not a default you inherited.
:::

## Why a local model rather than a hosted one

The model you will install is Chinese, developed by Alibaba. It is worth being
direct about that, because the reflex is to treat provenance as the security
question, and here it is not.

::: {.tight}
| | |
|---|---|
| **Open weights, on your machine** | It cannot send your data anywhere. There is no connection to send it over — and you can verify that rather than trust it: turn the wifi off and watch it keep working. |
| **A closed model behind an API** | Receives everything you type, by construction, wherever the company is domiciled. |
:::

::: {.step}
On the dimension people actually care about — *does my work leave this room* —
open weights running locally are the stronger guarantee, and the nationality of
the developer does not enter into it.
:::

## And why a small one

Qwen 2.5 Coder is a **vertical** model: specialised for code, and consequently
far better at code, for its size, than a general assistant many times larger.

::: {.tight}
- A 3-billion-parameter model on a laptop is not competitive with a frontier
  system at open-ended reasoning.
- At completing a pandas idiom, or explaining what a function does, it is
  entirely adequate.
:::

::: {.check}
Choosing a small specialised model over a large general one — and knowing which
tasks admit that trade — is the applied judgement that separates a sensible AI
deployment from an expensive one. It is also, almost exactly, the judgement
session 4 makes about a deliberately biased estimator.
:::

## 3 · Install VS Codium

Download from **[vscodium.com](https://vscodium.com)** and install it as you
would any application.

::: {.warn}
VS Codium uses the **Open VSX** registry rather than Microsoft's Marketplace.
Some extensions are missing from it. The two you need are both there.
:::

Install these from the Extensions panel (`Cmd/Ctrl + Shift + X`):

::: {.tight}
- **Python** — by Microsoft, on Open VSX as `ms-python.python`
- **Continue** — the assistant panel, which part 7 points at a model
:::

::: {.step}
From here on, **always use the VS Codium terminal** — `Ctrl + ` ` ` to open it.
Not the macOS Terminal, not PowerShell. It starts inside your project folder and
it sees your virtual environment.
:::

## A note on PATH that will save you an hour

A terminal reads your PATH **once, when it opens**. VS Codium reads it once,
when *it* opens, and every terminal tab inherits that copy.

::: {.tight}
| After installing | To make it visible |
|---|---|
| A **VS Codium extension** | *Developer: Reload Window* — `Cmd/Ctrl + Shift + P` |
| **Python** or **git** | Quit VS Codium entirely and reopen it |
| **Ollama** | A new terminal tab is usually enough — `+` in the terminal panel |
:::

::: {.muted}
"But I just installed it" is the single most common problem in this pre-session,
and it is almost always this.
:::

## 4 · Install Python

You want **3.12 or 3.13**. Anything older than 3.10 will fail on syntax used
throughout the course.

**macOS** — check what you have, then install if needed:

```bash
python3 --version
brew install python@3.12          # if Homebrew is installed
```

**Windows** — download the installer from [python.org](https://www.python.org/downloads/).

::: {.warn}
On Windows, tick **"Add python.exe to PATH"** on the first screen of the
installer. If you miss it, `python` will not be a command your terminal knows,
and the error message will not tell you why.
:::

**Linux** — you already have it. `python3 --version` to confirm.

## 5 · Make a virtual environment

A virtual environment is a folder holding one project's packages. It exists so
that installing something for this course cannot break something else on your
machine.

```bash
python3 -m venv .venv
source .venv/bin/activate          # macOS and Linux
.venv\Scripts\activate             # Windows
```

Your prompt now starts with `(.venv)`. That is the whole signal that it worked.

::: {.warn}
You must activate it **every time you open a new terminal**. Ninety per cent of
"it says the module is not installed" is a terminal where nobody ran `activate`.
:::

## 6 · Get the course, and check it works

```bash
git clone https://github.com/warint/essentials-data-science-python.git
cd essentials-data-science-python
source .venv/bin/activate
pip install -r requirements.txt
```

Then run the suite that checks the course data is intact:

```bash
python scripts/verify_puzzles.py
```

::: {.check}
You should see 39 lines beginning `[  ok  ]` and, at the end,
**All planted answers are present and all traps still spring.**
:::

::: {.muted}
It takes about twenty seconds. If a line says `FAIL`, bring the output to class —
that is a bug in the course, not in your setup.
:::

## What that suite just did

It generated all six course datasets and checked that each one still contains
the answer it is supposed to contain.

Every dataset in this course is **built on your machine from a fixed seed**.
Nothing is downloaded. Three things follow, and they shape how the sessions run:

::: {.tight}
- The practice works with the wifi off.
- Your numbers and your neighbour's numbers are **identical**, so if you
  disagree, one of you has made an analytical mistake — which is the useful kind
  of argument.
- There is a **right answer**, and you can check whether you found it.
:::

## 7 · Install Ollama and pull the model

Install **[ollama.com](https://ollama.com)**, then, in the VS Codium terminal:

```bash
ollama --version
ollama pull qwen2.5-coder:3b
```

Check that it answers:

```bash
ollama run qwen2.5-coder:3b "In one sentence, what is a residual?"
```

::: {.check}
**Now turn your wifi off and run that again.** It should still answer. That is
the whole point of running it locally, and it is worth seeing once with your own
eyes rather than taking on trust.
:::

::: {.muted}
`ollama: command not found` immediately after installing? Open a **new
terminal**. On Windows, quit VS Codium and reopen it — see the PATH slide.
:::

## Which size to pull

**Start with the 3b.** It is the one that works on a laptop without a dedicated
graphics card, which is most laptops.

| | 3b | 7b |
|---|---|---|
| **Disk** | 1.9 GB | 4.7 GB |
| **RAM while loaded** | ~3.4 GB | ~8 GB |
| **Needs a GPU** | no | not required, but painful without |

```bash
ollama pull qwen2.5-coder:7b     # only if the 3b already runs on the GPU
```

::: {.warn}
Only try the 7b once `ollama ps` reports **100% GPU** on the 3b. If it already
says 100% CPU, the 7b is not a better model on your machine — it gives a
comparable answer to the same question at roughly a quarter of the speed, and a
tool slow enough to interrupt your thinking is a tool you stop using.
:::

::: {.muted}
Whichever you pull, put **that exact name** in `config.yaml`. A name that is not
installed produces a confusing error rather than a missing-model one.
:::

::: {.muted}
Rule of thumb for any model: it needs its **file size plus about a fifth** in
memory.
:::

## Check the context window

The model is sent your file. If its context window is small it **silently drops
the beginning** and answers about the part it can still see — which looks like
stupidity rather than truncation.

```bash
ollama run qwen2.5-coder:3b "hi"
ollama ps
```

```text
NAME                SIZE      PROCESSOR    CONTEXT    UNTIL
qwen2.5-coder:3b    3.1 GB    100% GPU     32768      4 minutes from now
```

::: {.check}
**8192 or more — do nothing.** **2048 or 4096 — raise it** with
`/set parameter num_ctx 8192` inside `ollama run`, or via Ollama's settings.
:::

::: {.warn}
This differs by platform, so check rather than assume. The macOS app asks for a
large window and the model caps it at its own maximum. **On Windows the default
is often 4096**, which any real file will outgrow.
:::

## 8 · Point Continue at it

Continue is installed but talks to nothing until it has a config file. The
easiest way to open it is from inside Continue:

::: {.step}
Open the Continue panel → the **gear icon** at its top right → *Configure*. It
opens `config.yaml` in the editor, creating it if it does not exist.
:::

Or from the terminal — the file lives in your home directory:

```bash
mkdir -p ~/.continue && open -e ~/.continue/config.yaml            # macOS
mkdir -p ~/.continue && ${EDITOR:-nano} ~/.continue/config.yaml    # Linux
```

```powershell
New-Item -ItemType Directory -Force "$HOME\.continue" | Out-Null
notepad "$HOME\.continue\config.yaml"                              # Windows
```

## What to put in it

```yaml
name: essentials
version: 0.0.1
models:
  - name: Local coder
    provider: ollama
    model: qwen2.5-coder:3b     # the size you actually pulled
    roles: [chat, edit, apply]
context:
  - provider: file
  - provider: code
  - provider: diff
  - provider: terminal
```

::: {.check}
Open a `.py` file, select a few lines, and press `Cmd/Ctrl + L`. If the panel
answers, you are finished with setup for the whole term.
:::

::: {.warn}
Put the model name you **actually pulled** in `config.yaml`. A name that is not
installed produces a confusing error rather than a missing-model one.

Nothing at all? No model server is listening. Start Ollama — the app on macOS
and Windows, `sudo systemctl start ollama` on Linux.
:::

## What the model is for, and what it is not

You will read far more code this term than you write: the session decks, the
starter scripts, your own work from three weeks ago. A model beside the file
answers *"what does this do"* without your leaving the file.

::: {.tight}
| Good use | Poor use |
|---|---|
| "Explain what this block does" | "Write my analysis" |
| "Why does this throw a KeyError?" | "Is this result significant?" |
| "What is the pandas idiom for this?" | "Interpret this coefficient for me" |
:::

::: {.get}
**The standing rule of this course.** Every deliverable must document at least
one instance where you identified a model output as wrong, unverifiable or
misleading, and explain how you established that. You are never penalised for
using the model. You are penalised for using it uncritically.
:::

::: {.muted}
The honest limitation, stated once: on a machine without a graphics card, a
small model is a capable **reader** and an unreliable **editor**. It will explain
a function correctly and then fail to produce a well-formed multi-file edit,
because emitting a precise diff is a harder task than describing code. That is a
fact about small models rather than about you.
:::

## 9 · Enough pandas to start

Do this at the keyboard, not by reading. Activate the environment, then:

```python
import essentials as ess

ess.catalog()                     # the six datasets, and what each one asks
d = ess.load("coasters")          # session 1's data
```

Now look at it. These five are the ones you will use constantly:

```python
d.shape                           # (rows, columns)
d.head()                          # the first five rows
d.dtypes                          # what type each column is
d.describe()                      # count, mean, sd, quartiles, per column
d.columns.tolist()                # the names, as a list
```

## Selecting and filtering

```python
d["drop_m"]                       # one column, as a Series
d[["drop_m", "speed_kmh"]]        # two columns, as a DataFrame

d[d.drop_m > 100]                 # rows where the drop exceeds 100 m
d[d.propulsion == "gravity"]      # rows matching a string
d.query("drop_m > 100")           # the same filter, more readable
```

::: {.warn}
`d["drop_m"]` gives a Series; `d[["drop_m"]]` gives a one-column DataFrame. They
print almost identically and behave differently. The double bracket means
*"a list of columns"*, and the list happens to have one item in it.
:::

## Grouping, sorting, and new columns

```python
d.groupby("propulsion")["speed_kmh"].mean()      # a mean per group
d.groupby("propulsion").size()                   # how many in each group

d.sort_values("speed_kmh", ascending=False).head(5)

d["speed_ms"] = d.speed_kmh / 3.6                # a new column
```

::: {.check}
Before class, answer these three from the data, in Python:
how many coasters are there · what is the mean top speed by `propulsion` ·
which single coaster has the largest `drop_m`.
:::

## 10 · Enough inference to read a coefficient

A regression hands you three numbers per variable. You need to know what each
one is before you can be told a fourth.

| | |
|---|---|
| **Coefficient** | how much $y$ moves per one-unit move in $x$ — **in the units of $y$** |
| **Standard error** | how much that estimate would wobble if you collected the data again |
| **$t$-statistic** | the coefficient divided by its standard error: how many wobbles from zero |

::: {.step}
A coefficient is a quantity with units. A $t$-statistic is a ratio, and has
none. Reporting the second without the first is the most common way to say
nothing at all.
:::

## The $p$-value, stated carefully

> If the true effect were **exactly zero**, and I repeated this whole study many
> times, what fraction of those studies would produce a coefficient at least
> this far from zero?

That is the $p$-value. It is a statement about *data under an assumption*, not
about the probability that the assumption is true.

::: {.warn}
It does not tell you the effect is large. It does not tell you the effect is
real. With 2,000 rows, an effect too small to care about will clear $p < 0.05$
comfortably — and you would still be right not to care.
:::

## What $R^2$ is, and what it is not

$R^2$ is the share of the variance in $y$ that your fitted values reproduce.
It runs from 0 to 1, and it rises whenever you add a variable — including a
variable made of pure noise.

::: {.step}
$R^2$ measures how *close* the line is to the points. It says nothing about
whether the line is the **right shape**.
:::

::: {.warn}
Session 1's puzzle is built precisely on that gap: a model with $R^2 = 0.96$
that gets the answer wrong, sitting next to a model that gets it right. If you
learn one thing before class, learn to distrust that number on its own.
:::

## 12 · Self-check

On paper. If you cannot answer these, that is what the session is for.

::: {.tight}
1. A regression of salary on years of experience gives a coefficient of 2,400.
   What are its units, and what does the number mean in a sentence?
2. Two studies estimate the same effect. One reports $p = 0.04$, the other
   $p = 0.002$. What can you conclude about which effect is larger?
3. You add a column of random numbers to a regression. What happens to $R^2$,
   and why?
:::

::: {.muted}
Answer 2 is the interesting one, and the answer is "nothing at all".
:::

## 13 · What session 1 will ask of you

By the end of the session you should be able to:

::: {.tight}
- Fit a linear model from a formula and read every column of its output
- Say what a residuals-versus-fitted plot reveals, and what you looked for
- Compute leverage, and say which observations can move the line
- Separate an outlier from an **influential** point using Cook's distance
- Recognise when a straight line is fitting a curved relationship, and fix it
:::

::: {.get}
**Arrive with:** VS Codium open with the environment activated ·
`verify_puzzles.py` passing · Continue answering from a local model ·
chapters 2 and 3 read · the three pandas questions answered · the self-check
attempted on paper.
:::
